## Rule Precedence for Overlapping Principles

The principles above were derived independently and may overlap. The narrower condition is applied first, and each broader rule explicitly excludes the narrower cases. Labels "Principle 1" through "Principle 4" in Sections 1.1, 1.3, 1.5, and 1.9 refer to principles integrated in an earlier revision. "Moderation Principle 1" through "Moderation Principle 4" refer to principles integrated in the current revision: Moderation Principle 1 is in Section 1.10, Moderation Principle 2 is in the compositional form of Section 1.3, and Moderation Principles 3 and 4 are in Section 3.4. Where two rules would label the same span differently, apply them in this order:

1. **Composite Mention** (Section 2 and Section 2.1) overrides Sections 1.1 through 1.10 and Sections 3.3 and 3.4. A coordinated string naming two or more disorders is Composite, including inside population or family-history frames (e.g., "a family history of breast or ovarian cancer"). Composite spans follow their own definitions and are not treated as Section 1.4 feature glosses. Section 1.9(e) defers to this item.
2. **Modifier labelling** (Sections 3.1 and 3.2, and the attributive role of Section 3.4(b)) is determined before the Specific Disease and Disease Class tests are applied to the same span. A span labelled Modifier is excluded from Sections 1.1 through 1.10 and Section 3.3. Section 1.4 does not govern Modifier boundaries.
3. **Referent introduction** (Section 3.3) is applied only to spans not labelled Modifier under item 2. Its non-referential negative constraint returns population, case-set, patient-group, gene, and protein premodifiers to Modifier. It does not return prepositional complements to Modifier; those are governed by item 21.
4. **Name-versus-reference gate** (Section 1.7) is applied before any Specific Disease assignment. It blocks Specific Disease for anaphoric and descriptive-finding spans, but not for nosological naming frames under Section 1.8, patient-condition frames under Section 1.9, or eponym- and abbreviation-anchored names under Section 1.10 (item 19). It does not remove a Disease Class or Composite label established under another rule.
5. **Mechanism and measured-finding frames** (Section 1.5, "What NOT to Annotate," item 7, and Section 1.9(c) and (f)) are applied before Section 1.8. A deficiency introduced by a result or consequence construction, or a measured gene-product quantity, cannot be promoted to Specific Disease by Section 1.8 or Section 1.10. These frames also block the compositional Disease Class of item 20.
6. **Nosological naming** (Section 1.8) is applied before the feature-gloss test of Section 1.3 and before the named-entity test of Section 1.6. Within Section 1.8, the identity test in (a) is applied before the gloss test: a parenthetical that refers to the same disorder is **Specific Disease**, and one that adds a manifestation is **Disease Class**. Route (b) (sole defining phenotype) overrides Section 1.3 for nosological-state heads only, and does not apply to deficit heads with molecular complements (item 15). Items in a coordinated list remain under Section 1.3.
7. **Post-nominal molecular complements** (Section 1.5) are applied before Section 1.6 and before the fixed-compound rule (Section 1.2). Section 1.5 excludes compact fixed compounds (which go to Section 1.2 as Specific Disease) and adjectival forms (which are Modifier).
8. **Fixed-nomenclature compounds** (Section 1.2) assign Specific Disease to the whole string. Section 1.6 explicitly preserves these compounds.
9. **Named-entity versus category** (Section 1.6) applies after items 4 through 8, items 16, 18, and 19. Its free "X of Y" Disease Class trigger applies only where the complement does not form a recognized condition under Section 1.8(c). Its bare-category trigger also governs generic terms in prepositional complements (item 21).
10. **Referent over form** (Section 1.4) is applied before the generic-descriptor trigger in Section 1.3. Its case-level and alias Specific Disease triggers override the feature-position default. Its feature-gloss and "characterized by" Disease Class triggers agree with Section 1.3, including the manifestation-frame treatment of bare sign nouns.
11. **Individuated generic heads** (Section 1.1) override the bare-term exclusion in "What NOT to Annotate," item 4, only when the mention is individuated. Umbrella, enumerated, and anaphoric uses remain excluded.
12. **Biological-process nominals** ("What NOT to Annotate," item 5) override the pathological-process trigger in Section 1.3, the manifestation-frame treatment in Section 1.3, the deviation-operator paragraph of Section 1.3 (item 17), and the shared-head rule in Section 2.1(f). The exception is a deviation-qualified process nominal in a characterizing or causal pathological-outcome frame, which is labelled under item 20.
13. **Measured or mechanistic quantities** ("What NOT to Annotate," item 7) override the Section 1.3 trigger for gene-product activity, even when the activity appears in a "characterized by" list. They also override Section 1.8(b), Section 1.9(c), and Moderation Principle 2(c) (item 20).
14. **Named disorders** are governed by Sections 1 and 1.1, by Section 1.4 for lowercase common-noun forms, and by Section 1.8 for alias and naming forms. They are not governed by Section 1.3. Eponym- or site-named conditions are **Specific Disease**. Eponym-anchored finding nouns that name a condition by identity are governed by Section 1.10 (item 19).
15. **Deficit-construction span boundary** (Section 1.5, Principle 2) is the narrower condition for a deficit-type head with an "of" or "in" molecular complement. It is applied together with item 5, before items 6 and 16. It blocks Specific Disease on the deficit phrase and its molecular complement, so Section 1.8(b) and Section 1.9 cannot promote it. Its exemptions (lexicalized condition names, Section 1.8(c) recognized conditions, Section 1.8(a) identity aliases, disorder-naming heads, and non-molecular complements) return the span to the Specific Disease rules. This item does not alter Disease Class decisions, including the compositional form of item 20.
16. **Finding- or state-anchored named-target mentions** (Section 1.9, Principle 1) is the broader condition. It is applied after items 4, 5, 13, and 15. It is excluded for assay, measured, mechanism, result-frame, and lexicalized-head cases, and for deficit-with-molecular-complement cases unless item 15's exemption applies. A result-frame exclusion does not apply where the finding noun is the condition's own label (item 19). It does not override Composite Mention (item 1).
17. **Deviation-operator Disease Class** (Section 1.3, deviation paragraph, Principle 3) is applied after items 4, 9, 14, and 16, so that Specific Disease assignments, lexicalized names, and recognized conditions are not relabelled. It is excluded for biological-process heads except as item 20 provides (item 12), for molecular complements of deficit nominals except where item 20 applies to a clinical characterizing feature (items 5, 7, and 15), for measured values (item 13), and for causal mutation, variant, or agent frames ("What NOT to Annotate," item 8). Item 20 is the compositional extension of this item.
18. **Etiology-anchored condition mentions** (Section 1.1, etiology paragraph, Principle 4) are Specific Disease assignments. They are applied before the bare-head and "X of Y" defaults of Section 1.6, and they yield to the manifestation-list convention (item 10) and the umbrella exclusions (item 11). Inheritance-pattern qualifiers do not trigger them.
19. **Named conditions without a nosological head** (Section 1.10, Moderation Principle 1) are applied after items 1 through 3, 13, 15, and 16, and before item 9. Where the item-16 frame governs, its label stands. This item applies Specific Disease to eponym-, finding-noun-, and abbreviation-anchored names with non-disease heads. It yields to item 2 (Modifier), to item 5 (measured and mechanistic frames), and to the exclusions of Section 1.10 (gene-level, enzyme-level, laboratory, broad-category, and Modifier-only spans).
20. **Compositional pathological-state Disease Class** (Section 1.3, Moderation Principle 2) is applied after items 4, 13, and 15. It is the compositional extension of item 17. It takes precedence over the process-nominal exclusion of item 12 for deviation-qualified process heads in characterizing or causal outcome frames. It yields: (a) to Section 1.5 and item 5 for molecular complements in a mechanism or result-introduced frame, which is the narrower gene-product rule and is not reopened by the "results in" trigger; (b) to item 13 for measured values, experimental manipulations, and reagent states; (c) to item 1 for coordinated multi-condition mentions; (d) to item 8 for causal agents; and (e) to item 4 and Section 1.4 for lexicalized names. Normal or non-deviation process nominals remain excluded.
21. **Prepositional-complement and syntactic-role test** (Section 3.4; Moderation Principles 3 and 4) is applied after items 1 and 2. It decides Modifier versus non-Modifier status and, within non-Modifier mentions, between Specific Disease and Disease Class. Where a generic category term sits in a prepositional complement, the narrower bare-category rule of Section 1.6(a) and Moderation Principle 3 yields Disease Class. It governs before the broader syntactic-role default of Moderation Principle 4, which would otherwise yield Specific Disease. Gene- and protein-premodifier Modifier labels (Section 3.1) and Composite spans remain above this item.

Where a rule states that it does not apply to a case handled by another rule, that exclusion is binding. The narrower rule is applied first.

---

## What NOT to Annotate

1. **Do not annotate organism names**  
   - Organism names such as "human" were excluded from the preferred mention.  
   - Viruses, bacteria, and other organism names were not annotated **unless** it was clear that the disease caused by these organisms is being discussed.  
   - **Example**  
     > Studies of biopsied tissue for the presence of Epstein-Barr virus and cytomegalovirus were negative.  
     
     In this case: "Epstein-Barr virus" and "cytomegalovirus" are annotated as **Specific Disease** category **only** if the context clearly indicates the diseases they cause, otherwise not.

2. **Do not annotate gender**  
   - Tokens such as "male" and "female" were only included if they specifically identified a new form of the disease.  
   - **Example**  
     > "male breast cancer"

3. **Do not annotate overlapping mentions**  
   - **Example**: The phrase "von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease" is annotated as **one single disease mention** (Specific Disease category).  
   - Running-text alternative names that co-refer to the same condition are not annotated as separate mentions (Section 1.4).  
   - Parenthetical, appositive, or alias-marked alternative names that pass the identity test are **Specific Disease** mentions under Section 1.8(a), and are annotated as separate mentions like abbreviations (Section 6). Parenthetical glosses that add a manifestation rather than naming the disorder are **Disease Class** (Section 1.3).

4. **Do not annotate general terms**  
   - Very general terms such as "disease," "syndrome," "deficiency," "complications," "abnormalities," etc. are excluded when used bare or as unspecified umbrella placeholders.  
   - These terms are annotated when they refer to one individuated condition (Section 1.1), or when they are part of a specific name (e.g., "C7 deficiency," Section 1.2).  
   - Anaphoric or demonstrative placeholders that point back to a condition named elsewhere (e.g., "this condition," "such disorder") are not annotated (Section 1.7).  
   - However, the terms "cancer" and "tumor" were retained. A bare, generic "cancer" in a prepositional complement (e.g., "a family history of cancer") is **Disease Class** (Section 3.4(a)).

5. **Do not annotate references to biological processes**  
   - Terms corresponding to biological processes such as "tumorigenesis" or "cancerogenesis" are not annotated.  
   - Process nominals (e.g., "development," "accumulation") are not annotated when they are neutral or normal, including when they occur with no deviation marker, because they describe mechanisms rather than states of the patient (Section 1.3).  
   - A process nominal preceded by a deviation marker and used as the argument of a characterizing or causal pathological-outcome predicate is **not** excluded. It is labelled **Disease Class** under the compositional form of Section 1.3 (Moderation Principle 2; Rule Precedence, items 12 and 20). For example, "abnormal retinal vascular development" after "is characterized by" (Example 27).  
   - This exclusion also applies within coordinated anatomical modifiers unless Moderation Principle 2 labels the full span (Section 2.1(f)).

6. **Do not annotate disease mentions interrupted by nested mentions**  
   - Essentially, do not break the contiguous text rule.  
   - **Example**  
     > WT1 dysfunction is implicated in both neoplastic (Wilms tumor, mesothelioma, leukemia, and breast cancer) and nonneoplastic (glomerulosclerosis) disease.  
     
     Here, the mentions "neoplastic disease" and "nonneoplastic disease" are not annotated because other tokens break up these phrases. A parenthetical between coordinated modifiers also blocks Section 2.1 (Section 2.1(e)).

7. **Do not annotate mechanistic, biochemical, or experimental quantities**  
   - Measured properties of a gene product or experimental system, such as specific activity, enzyme yield, thermal stability, expression level, or measured deficient activity (e.g., "deficient activity of FALDH"), are not annotated, even when they appear in a characterizing list (Sections 1.3 and 1.7; Section 1.8 exclusions; Moderation Principle 2(c)).  
   - Post-nominal molecular complements that describe a mechanism (e.g., "a deficiency of norrin within the developing retina") are likewise not annotated (Section 1.5).  
   - The exception is a phrase that names a condition under Section 1.2 (fixed nomenclature compound), Section 1.8 (naming frame, including a recognized clinical condition under Section 1.8(c)), Section 1.9 (patient-condition frame that is not excluded by its own negative conditions), or Section 1.10 (named condition by identity).

8. **Do not annotate causal etiological agents, even inside a deviation or pathological frame.**  
   - Mutations, variants, alterations, polymorphisms, expansions, and exposures are not annotated as **Disease Class** merely because a deviation term or pathological outcome is attached to them (Section 1.3, deviation paragraph; Principle 3).  
   - **Example:** "somatic mutation in the NDP gene" (Example 29) and "germline BRCA1 alterations" are not annotated.  
   - A named disorder that is the outcome of such an agent is annotated under its own rules.

---

## Examples

1. **"Insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus"**  
   - **Specific Disease**  
   - Prefer the whole string.

2. **CDH1 mutations predispose to early onset "colorectal cancer."**  
   - "early onset" may or may not be part of the disease mention, depending on:  
     1. If there is a UMLS concept specifying this as a separate form of disease  
     2. If the annotator believes it should be included

3. **Human "X-linked recessive disorder"**  
   - Category-level inheritance modifier; **Disease Class** (Section 1.1).

4. **Her fresh serum lacked complement-mediated bactericidal activity against Neisseria gonorrhoeae.**  
   - Measured functional activity with no condition name; not annotated (Section 1.7; Section 1.9(c); "What NOT to Annotate," item 7).

5. **"Huntington disease" ("HD")**  
   - The long form and the short form constitute two separate mentions.

6. **C7 deficiency**  
   - "This report represents the first cases of C7 deficiency associated with infectious complications."  
   - "C7 deficiency" is a **Specific Disease** (fixed nomenclature compound; Section 1.2).  
   - "infectious complications" is an unspecified umbrella term and is not annotated, even though it is a consequence argument (Section 1.3; "What NOT to Annotate," item 4).

7. **"colorectal, endometrial, and ovarian cancers"**  
   - Considered one **Composite Mention** of several Specific Diseases.

8. **WT1 dysfunction is implicated in both neoplastic ("Wilms tumor," "mesothelioma," "leukemias," and "breast cancer") and nonneoplastic ("glomerulosclerosis") disease.**  
   - Potential disease mentions include: "neoplastic disease," "nonneoplastic disease," "Wilms tumor," "mesothelioma," "leukemias," "breast cancer," and "glomerulosclerosis."  
   - "neoplastic disease" and "nonneoplastic disease" are **not** annotated because these phrases are interrupted by nested mentions.

9. **Tumorigenesis and cancerogenesis**  
   - These refer to processes, not diseases.

10. **"autosomal recessive disease"**  
    - Refers to a family of diseases that can be passed down genetically → **Disease Class** category.  
    - The inheritance-pattern modifier does not anchor the mention to one condition (Section 1.1).

11. **Large phenotypic variability with "convulsive disorders," "motor retardation," and "mental retardation."**  
    - These are "grey area" terms: they may not correspond to a single **Specific Disease**, so they are annotated as **Disease Class** category if appropriate.  
    - Items in an enumeration are not individuated (Section 1.1). Established disorder terms such as "mental retardation" keep the **Disease Class** label.

12. **Borjeson-Forssman-Lehmann syndrome (BFLS) is a syndromal X-linked mental retardation.**  
    - "Borjeson-Forssman-Lehmann syndrome" = **Specific Disease**  
    - "X-linked mental retardation syndrome" = a family of diseases (i.e., **Disease Class**)

13. **Acute meningococcal pericarditis**  
    - Exists as a separate concept in UMLS.

14. **Acute Neisseria infection**  
    - May or may not include "acute" depending on context.  
    - When the infection is diagnosed in a patient, the etiology-anchored rule of Section 1.1 (Principle 4) applies to "Neisseria infection."

15. **Classical galactosemia**  
    - Includes "classical" because it corresponds to a particular form of the disease (Section 1.1).

16. **Inherited spinocerebellar ataxia**  
    - May or may not include "inherited," depending on the annotator.

17. **"Adenomatous polyps of the colon and rectum"**  
    - **Composite Mention**

18. **Fibroepithelial or epithelial hyperplasias**  
    - **Composite Mention** (Section 2.1).

19. **Stage II or stage III colorectal cancer**  
    - **Composite Mention** (Section 2.1).

20. **"Patients with deficiency of adenosine deaminase presented with recurrent infections."**  
    - "deficiency of adenosine deaminase" as **Specific Disease**: the enzyme complement forms a recognized clinical condition, and the phrase names that condition in a case-level presentation frame (Sections 1.2, 1.4, and 1.8(c)).  
    - The span-boundary rule of Section 1.5 does not block this label because the whole string is a conventional lexicalized condition name (Rule Precedence, item 15).  
    - The compact fixed form "adenosine deaminase deficiency" is also **Specific Disease** as a whole string.  
    - A mechanistic use of the same head-plus-complement is not annotated (Example 30).

21. **"the G6PD deficient phenotype"**  
    - "G6PD deficient" as **Modifier**; the privative adjective modifies a phenotype (Sections 1.2 and 3.2).

22. **"ancient SLS genes"**  
    - "SLS" as **Modifier**; the head denotes a class of genes (Section 3.1).

23. **"breast cancer susceptibility gene 1 (BRCA1)"**  
    - "breast cancer" as **Modifier**; "gene 1 (BRCA1)" is unannotated (Section 3.1).

24. **"ovarian cancer cases," "ovarian cancer population"**  
    - "ovarian cancer" as **Modifier**. The head is clinical or epidemiological, so Section 3.1 applies, and the non-referential negative constraint of Section 3.3 applies.

25. **"The proband was diagnosed with an X-linked disorder."**  
    - "X-linked disorder" as **Specific Disease** (patient-diagnosis framing; Section 1.1).  
    - Contrast with Example 3, where the same modifier names a category.

26. **"Disorder X is characterized by mental retardation, seizures, and hypotonia."** (illustrative)  
    - "Disorder X" as **Specific Disease**.  
    - "mental retardation" as **Disease Class** (established disorder term; Sections 1.3 and 1.4).  
    - "seizures" and "hypotonia" as **Disease Class**: bare sign nouns occupying a "characterized by" list (manifestation frame; Sections 1.3 and 1.4).

27. **"Coats disease is characterized by abnormal retinal vascular development, which results in massive intraretinal and subretinal lipid accumulation."**  
    - "Coats disease" as **Specific Disease**.  
    - "abnormal retinal vascular development" as **Disease Class**: a deviation-qualified process nominal that is the argument of a characterizing predicate ("characterized by"; Moderation Principle 2; Rule Precedence, item 20).  
    - "massive intraretinal and subretinal lipid accumulation" as **Disease Class**: an excess-qualified substrate with coordinated anatomical modifiers, which is the outcome argument of "results in." The coordinated modifiers do not make it Composite (Section 2.1(f)). The bare "lipid accumulation" is not labelled on its own.

28. **"Specific activity and enzyme yield were measured for each recombinant variant."**  
    - No annotation. These are experimental quantities with no disorder framing, patient reference, or condition name ("What NOT to Annotate," item 7).

29. **"Coats' disease of the retina (unilateral retinal telangiectasis) caused by somatic mutation in the NDP gene…"**  
    - "Coats' disease" as **Specific Disease** (eponym).  
    - "unilateral retinal telangiectasis" as **Specific Disease**: a parenthetical alias that passes the identity test (Section 1.8(a); Section 6). It is a separate mention, as with an abbreviation.  
    - "somatic mutation in the NDP gene" is an etiologic agent and is not annotated (Section 1.3; "What NOT to Annotate," item 8).

30. **"…which results in a deficiency of norrin (the protein product of the NDP gene) within the developing retina."**  
    - "deficiency of norrin" is unannotated: a molecular complement in a result-introduced mechanism frame (Sections 1.3, 1.5, and 1.8 exclusions). The bare state noun is not labelled as a disease.  
    - The compositional form of Section 1.3 does not relabel it. The complement is a gene product in a mechanism frame, which Section 1.5 governs (Rule Precedence, item 20(a)). The span-boundary rule of Section 1.5 and the deviation exclusions of Section 1.3 also apply, as does Section 1.9(f).  
    - The parenthetical glosses a protein, not a disease, so it is not an alias under Section 1.8(a).

31. **"Sjogren-Larsson syndrome (SLS) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by ichthyosis, mental retardation, spasticity, and deficient activity of fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase (FALDH)."**  
    - "Sjogren-Larsson syndrome" and "SLS" as **Specific Disease** (eponym and acronym; Section 3.3).  
    - "autosomal recessive disorder" as **Disease Class** (Example 10).  
    - "mental retardation" as **Disease Class** (established disorder term; Example 11).  
    - "ichthyosis" and "spasticity" as **Disease Class**: bare sign nouns in a "characterized by" list (Sections 1.3 and 1.4).  
    - "deficient activity of FALDH" is a measured activity and is unannotated (Section 1.8 exclusion; "What NOT to Annotate," item 7; Rule Precedence, item 13; Moderation Principle 2(c)). It is also excluded by the span-boundary rule of Section 1.5 and by Section 1.9(c).  
    - The "severe reduction of FALDH enzyme catalytic activity" in the mutation-expression sentence of the same abstract is likewise unannotated (Moderation Principle 2(c)).

32. **"Coats disease is characterized by abnormal retinal vascular development (so-called retinal telangiectasis), which results in massive intraretinal and subretinal lipid accumulation (exudative retinal detachment)."**  
    - "Coats disease" as **Specific Disease**.  
    - "retinal telangiectasis" as **Specific Disease**: an identity alias introduced by an alias marker; "so-called" is not part of the span (Section 1.8(a)).  
    - "abnormal retinal vascular development" as **Disease Class**, and "massive intraretinal and subretinal lipid accumulation" as **Disease Class**, under the compositional form (Moderation Principle 2; Example 27).  
    - "exudative retinal detachment" as **Disease Class**: the identity test fails, so this parenthetical is a feature gloss of the disorder's pathology (Sections 1.3 and 1.4).

33. **"Two patients had Coats disease. This condition was bilateral in one."**  
    - "Coats disease" as **Specific Disease**.  
    - "This condition" is anaphoric and points back to the antecedent. It is not annotated as **Specific Disease** (Section 1.7; "What NOT to Annotate," item 4).

34. **"Both patients had a family history of breast or ovarian cancer."**  
    - "breast or ovarian cancer" as one **Composite Mention** (Section 2.1). The coordinated pre-head modifiers share the head "cancer."  
    - The family-history frame does not convert the string to **Modifier** (Section 3.4(a); Composite precedence applies; Rule Precedence, item 1). Moderation Principle 3 does not split or relabel the coordinated string.

35. **"…massive intraretinal and subretinal lipid accumulation…" (standalone fragment)**  
    - Not annotated when it appears as a standalone fragment with no characterizing or causal predicate (Moderation Principle 2(iii)).  
    - The coordinated anatomical modifiers do not form a Composite Mention, because the shared head is a process nominal (Section 2.1(f)).  
    - In Example 27, where the same phrase is the outcome argument of "results in," it is **Disease Class** under Moderation Principle 2.

36. **"Autoinhibition and activation mechanisms of the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein." and "…activation of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASP) family members…"**  
    - "Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome" as **Modifier** (Section 3.1). The determiner "the" does not make it **Specific Disease**, because Section 3.1 takes precedence over Section 3.3(i).  
    - "protein (WASP)" is unannotated.  
    - The autoinhibition and activation vocabulary describes a regulatory mechanism, not a pathological outcome, so the deviation paragraph of Section 1.3 does not apply.

37. **"…in the ovarian cancer population…," "…a population-based series of ovarian cancer cases…," "…a family history of ovarian cancer…," "…a family history of cancer…"**  
    - "ovarian cancer" as **Modifier** in the first two: attributive premodifiers of population and case-set heads (Section 3.3, negative constraint; Section 3.4(b)).  
    - "ovarian cancer" as **Specific Disease** in the third: the prepositional complement of "of," naming a particular disease (Moderation Principles 3 and 4; Section 3.4(a)).  
    - "cancer" as **Disease Class** in the fourth: a bare, generic category term in a prepositional complement (Moderation Principle 3; Section 1.6(a)).

38. **"…in probands from 63 kindreds with SLS."**  
    - "SLS" as **Specific Disease** (Section 3.3(iii)): a prepositional complement that names the condition the probands have. This differs from Example 37's first case because the disease string is not a premodifier of a population head.

39. **"We infer that the coexistence of the two mutations is responsible for enzyme deficiency in G6PD A-…"**  
    - "enzyme deficiency in G6PD A-" is unannotated: a mechanistic and biochemical deficiency in a causal frame (Sections 1.5 and 1.8 exclusions; "What NOT to Annotate," item 7). The span-boundary rule of Section 1.5 also applies, and the causal frame does not license tagging.  
    - "G6PD A-" names an enzyme variant, not a disease, and is not annotated here. Contrast with the compact "G6PD deficiency" (Example 21 family; Section 1.2), which is **Specific Disease**.

40. **Finding-anchored named target (Section 1.9).**  
    - (Illustrative) "The proband presented with a Lhermitte sign." → "Lhermitte sign" as **Specific Disease**: an eponym premodifier on a finding noun, presented as the patient's clinical condition.  
    - (Non-example) "Hypermethylation suppressed transcription, resulting in absence of the FMR1 protein." → not annotated. This is a mechanism or result frame (Section 1.9(f); Section 1.5). "Absence" is a deviation noun with a molecular complement in a causal frame, so the deviation paragraph of Section 1.3 excludes it, and the span-boundary rule of Section 1.5 excludes the molecular complement.

41. **Deficit-construction span boundary (Section 1.5; Principle 2).**  
    - (Illustrative; hypothetical names) "The proband was diagnosed with Smith syndrome, which is caused by a heterozygous deficiency of XYZ1 protein." → "Smith syndrome" as **Specific Disease** (patient diagnosis; Section 1.1).  
    - "heterozygous deficiency of XYZ1 protein" is not annotated. It is a deficit head with a molecular complement; the genotype and causal cues do not license tagging; and route (b) of Section 1.8 cannot promote it (Rule Precedence, item 15).

42. **Compositional and deviation-operator Disease Class (Section 1.3; Moderation Principle 2).**  
    - (Illustrative) "Disorder Y is associated with abnormal retinal vasculature and abnormal retinal vascular development. Normal retinal vascular development was preserved in unaffected siblings."  
    - "Disorder Y" as **Specific Disease**.  
    - "abnormal retinal vasculature" as **Disease Class** (anatomical-structure head with a deviation qualifier in a characterizing frame).  
    - "abnormal retinal vascular development" as **Disease Class** (process substrate with a deviation marker in a characterizing frame; Moderation Principle 2).  
    - "Normal retinal vascular development" is not annotated: no deviation marker (Moderation Principle 2(b); "What NOT to Annotate," item 5).

43. **Etiology-anchored condition (Section 1.1; Principle 4).**  
    - (Illustrative) "A streptococcal infection was diagnosed in the proband." → "streptococcal infection" as **Specific Disease**: the modifier is derived from a single named causal organism, the head is a generic condition noun, and the condition is diagnosed in a patient.  
    - Contrast with Example 10, where "autosomal recessive" is an inheritance pattern and does not anchor the mention to one condition.

44. **Finding noun as alternate label (Section 1.10(b); Moderation Principle 1).**  
    - "We suggest that Coats telangiectasis is secondary to somatic mutation in the NDP gene which results in a deficiency of norrin (the protein product of the NDP gene) within the developing retina."  
    - "Coats telangiectasis" as **Specific Disease**: a finding noun used as an alternate label for the eponymous condition Coats disease, named earlier in the document. The "secondary to" frame does not exclude it, because the finding names the condition rather than a mechanism (Section 1.9(f); Section 1.10 relation).  
    - "somatic mutation in the NDP gene" is an etiologic agent and is not annotated ("What NOT to Annotate," item 8).  
    - "deficiency of norrin" is not annotated (Example 30).

45. **Bare abbreviation with a document-level expansion (Section 1.10(c); Moderation Principle 1).**  
    - "Our results demonstrate that SLS is caused by a strikingly heterogeneous group of mutations in the FALDH gene…" → "SLS" as **Specific Disease**: a bare abbreviation whose expansion ("Sjogren-Larsson syndrome") appears in the title, used as the subject of a condition frame.  
    - "All of the patients with SLS were found to carry mutations" → "SLS" as **Specific Disease** (prepositional complement; Section 3.4(b)).  
    - "ancient SLS genes" → "SLS" as **Modifier** (premodifier of a gene head; Section 3.1). The Section 1.10 exclusion for Modifier-only spans applies.

46. **Prepositional complement and syntactic role (Section 3.4; Moderation Principles 3 and 4).**  
    - "…some of which were associated with a family history of cancer." → "cancer" as **Disease Class**: a bare, generic category term in a prepositional complement (Moderation Principle 3; Section 1.6(a)).  
    - "…suggesting that this polymorphism may influence ovarian cancer risk." → "ovarian cancer" as **Modifier**: an attributive premodifier of a non-disease head ("risk") (Moderation Principle 3, modifier scope).  
    - "Both patients had a family history of breast or ovarian cancer." → one **Composite Mention** (Example 34).

47. **Gene-product deficit in a result-introduced mechanism frame (Moderation Principle 2(e); Section 1.5).**  
    - "…suppresses transcription, resulting in absence of the FMR1 protein." → "absence of the FMR1 protein" is not annotated: a gene-product deficit introduced by a result construction. Section 1.5 governs, and the "results in" trigger of Moderation Principle 2 does not reopen it.  
    - "full mutation" (the expanded CGG repeat) is a causal agent and is not annotated ("What NOT to Annotate," item 8).  
    - "fragile X syndrome" in "Most fragile X syndrome patients…" is a **Modifier** (premodifier of a patient-group head; Moderation Principle 4).

48. **Argument role in a complement of "of" or "by" (Section 3.4(b); Moderation Principle 4).**  
    - "…A female with a unilateral variant of Coats disease gave birth to a son affected by Norrie disease." → "Coats disease" as **Specific Disease** (complement of "of," naming a particular condition) and "Norrie disease" as **Specific Disease** (complement of "by"). Neither is a **Modifier**, although "unilateral variant" and "affected" frame them as attributes. The argument role governs.

### 1. Gold: SpecificDisease vs LLM: O (Missed) (8 cases)
## Step 1: Deep Dive Analysis

**Contrast.** The strongest evidence comes from comparing discrepancies and true positives within the same document:

- **Doc 10484772:** "Coats disease" (TP) is tagged, but "Coats telangiectasis" (FN) is missed. Both use the same eponym, so the difference is the head noun: *disease* versus *telangiectasis*, a sign term.
- **Doc 10577908:** "SLS" (TP) is tagged because it is anchored by the adjacent expansion "Sjogren-Larsson syndrome ( SLS )". "deficient activity of fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase" (FN) has no nosological head and no anchor.

The boolean feature that separates the cases is whether the disease mention carries a **nosological head** (disease, syndrome, cancer, a suffix like -uria) or is **anchored to one** by an adjacent expansion.

**Isolate Trigger.** The model appears to read these strings as mechanism, finding, or abbreviation text rather than as disease names:
- *"deficiency of / deficient activity of / deficiency in [enzyme or gene]"* is read as a molecular cause. In Example 4 the phrase is grammatically the object of "caused by," which reinforces the cause reading.
- *"telangiectasis"* is read as a clinical sign, even though the source text uses "retinal telangiectasis" as an alternate name for the disease.
- *"PKU"* is a bare acronym. Its expansion (phenylketonuria) appears elsewhere in the document, not in the local window.

**Hypothesis Check.** The single feature explains all five cases:
- Ex 2, 3, 4: no nosological head. The head is a deficiency or activity noun, and the disorder is named only through its enzyme.
- Ex 1: the head is a sign noun, not a condition noun.
- Ex 5: no head and no local expansion.

One caveat: the gold standard labels enzyme-deficiency spans as SpecificDisease, which is only defensible when the deficiency is the disorder's defining feature. That makes the rule conditional, not a blanket rule for all "deficiency of X" phrases.

## Step 2: Formulate Pattern

- **Pattern Insight: Disease Named Without a Nosological Head (Molecular Defect, Sign Term, or Unanchored Acronym)**
  - **Confusion Trigger:** Disease mentions whose surface head is not a disease-class noun. These include (a) "deficiency/deficient activity of/in [gene or enzyme]" phrases where the enzyme is the grammatical object, (b) a clinical sign noun ("telangiectasis") used in place of "disease," and (c) a bare acronym with no adjacent expansion. The model defaults to O, treating these as mechanism, finding, or abbreviation text.
  - **Contrastive Evidence:** The true positives carry an explicit nosological head ("Coats disease," "Norrie disease," "Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome," "fragile X syndrome," "ovarian cancer") or an adjacent expansion ("SLS"). Within the same documents, the eponym "Coats" and the acronym "SLS" are tagged when the head or expansion is present and missed when it is not.
  - **Linguistic Rule (Proposed):** For any candidate disease string, first check for a nosological head (disease, syndrome, disorder, cancer, -uria/-emia) or an adjacent parenthetical expansion. If neither is present, do not default to O:
    1. If the string is "deficiency/deficient activity of/in [gene or enzyme]" and the sentence presents it as the disorder's defining cause or feature (e.g., "a disease caused by a deficiency of…"), label the full span SpecificDisease.
    2. If a sign term is used as an alternate name for an eponymous disease already named in the document (e.g., "Coats telangiectasis" alongside "Coats disease"), label it SpecificDisease.
    3. If a bare acronym's expansion appears anywhere in the document as a disease name, label the acronym SpecificDisease.

### 2. Gold: DiseaseClass vs LLM: O (Missed) (2 cases)
**Step 1: Deep Dive Analysis**

- **Contrast:** The true-positive DiseaseClass example, "mental retardation," is a self-contained, lexicalized clinical condition label. The discrepant spans are compositional descriptions. Each is a qualifier applied to a normal biological substrate: "abnormal" + "retinal vascular development," and "deficiency of" + "norrin." The single boolean feature that separates them is whether the span **names a condition as a unit** or **describes a deviation from a normal biological entity or process**.
- **Isolate Trigger:** The model appears to read the head nouns literally. "Development" is a physiological process noun, and "norrin" is a protein (outside the schema). Both spans look like ordinary developmental biology or molecular biochemistry, so the model tags them O. The deviation qualifiers ("abnormal," "deficiency of") are the cues that make them pathological, and the model does not weigh them enough. "Deficiency of X" is especially ambiguous, since it is common biochemical phrasing for molecular states that are not diseases.
- **Hypothesis Check:** Both discrepancies sit in causal or characterizing predicates. The first follows "Coats disease is characterized by…" and the second follows "results in a…" in a pathogenesis explanation. Both are phenotypic or pathogenic states expressed compositionally, with no disease-name head. This explains both examples. The true positive, "mental retardation," has no qualifier-plus-substrate structure, which is consistent with the hypothesis.

**Step 2: Formulate Pattern**

- **Pattern Insight:**
  - **Pattern Name:** Compositional Pathological-State Descriptions (Deviation-from-Normal Noun Phrases)
  - **Confusion Trigger:** A deviation qualifier ("abnormal," "deficiency of") modifies a generic biological substrate (a process or gene product such as "vascular development" or "norrin"). The head noun is physiological or molecular, not a disease name, so the model treats the span as normal biology rather than a DiseaseClass mention.
  - **Contrastive Evidence:** The true-positive DiseaseClass, "mental retardation," is a lexicalized condition label with no qualifier-plus-substrate construction, so the model recognizes it as a unit. The Modifier true positives ("ovarian cancer," "Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome") are also named disease entities rather than compositional descriptions.
  - **Linguistic Rule (Proposed):** Tag the full noun phrase as DiseaseClass when a deviation-from-normal qualifier (abnormal, deficiency of, absence of, excess of) applied to a biological substrate denotes a pathological condition or state, and the phrase is the object of a disease-characterization or pathogenesis predicate (characterized by, results in, secondary to, caused by). Include the qualifier in the span. Do not tag the bare substrate (e.g., "norrin," "NDP gene") or a normal physiological process described without a deviation qualifier.

### 3. Gold: DiseaseClass vs LLM: Modifier (Label Mismatch) (1 cases)
**Step 1: Deep Dive Analysis**

- **Contrast:** The single feature that separates the control Modifiers from the discrepancy is syntactic slot. Every correct Modifier in the control set is a disease name used as an attributive premodifier directly before a non-disease head noun: "ovarian cancer **population**," "ovarian cancer **cases**," "ovarian cancer **study**," "ovarian cancer **risk**," "fragile X syndrome **patients**," "ancient SLS **genes**," "Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome **protein**." The discrepancy's "cancer" is the head of a prepositional complement ("history **of** cancer") and does not premodify anything.
- **Isolate Trigger:** "Family history of ___" is a qualifier-like construction that describes relatives or patients, so it resembles the Modifier function semantically. The model appears to have keyed on that qualifier meaning plus the token "cancer," which is inside most Modifier spans in this document, rather than on the syntactic slot. The bare "cancer" is also a generic category term, which points to DiseaseClass.
- **Hypothesis Check:** The premodifier rule explains the discrepancy, but it is not sufficient alone. Disease heads in complement positions still receive entity types, and those depend on specificity. "Classical form of **Coats disease**" and "affected by **Norrie disease**" are SpecificDisease, while "family history of **cancer**" is DiseaseClass. The pattern therefore needs a two-step refinement. No control-set Modifier matches the "family history of [disease]" construction, which supports treating it as a non-Modifier case.

**Step 2: Formulated Pattern**

- **Pattern Name:** Qualifier-Phrase Disease Noun Mislabeled as Modifier ("family history of [disease]")
- **Confusion Trigger:** A bare, generic disease noun ("cancer") serves as the complement of a qualifier-like prepositional phrase ("family history of ___"). The model treats the phrase's descriptive, patient/relative-status function as a Modifier and over-generalizes from the lexical co-occurrence of "cancer" with Modifier spans in the same document.
- **Contrastive Evidence:** Correct Modifier labels occur only when the disease name is an attributive premodifier before a head noun ("ovarian cancer risk," "ovarian cancer cases," "fragile X syndrome patients," "SLS genes"). Disease nouns in complement positions are labeled by specificity instead: "Norrie disease" and "Coats disease" become SpecificDisease, and the generic "mental retardation" in a symptom list becomes DiseaseClass. None of the correct Modifier cases involve a "history of" or "form of" complement.
- **Linguistic Rule (Proposed):**
  1. Label a disease term as **Modifier** only if it is an attributive premodifier immediately preceding a non-disease head noun (e.g., population, cases, study, risk, patients, genes, protein). Qualifier semantics ("history of," "risk of," "form of") do not license the Modifier label.
  2. If the term is not a premodifier, decide by specificity. A named, specific disease (Coats disease, Norrie disease, SLS, Sjogren-Larsson syndrome) is **SpecificDisease**. A generic or unspecified category term with no named type (bare "cancer," "mental retardation") is **DiseaseClass**.
  3. Applied here: "family history of **cancer**" has "cancer" as a PP complement and no named type, so it is **DiseaseClass**.
  4. Caveat: this rule is derived from one discrepancy. It should be checked against other "history of [disease]" and bare "cancer" mentions in Modifier-heavy documents before it is adopted.

### 4. Gold: SpecificDisease vs LLM: Modifier (Label Mismatch) (1 cases)
**Step 1: Deep Dive Analysis**

- **Contrast:** In the True Positives, the Modifier spans ("ovarian cancer population," "ovarian cancer cases," "ovarian cancer study," "fragile X syndrome patients," "ancient SLS genes," "Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein") are all **prenominal**. The disease string sits directly before a head noun and attributes a property to it. The SpecificDisease spans ("Coats disease is characterized," "affected by Norrie disease," "patients with SLS") are **heads of their own NP or complements of a preposition or verb**, where they name the condition itself.
- **Isolate Trigger:** In Example 1, "ovarian cancer" is the object of "of" in "a family history of ovarian cancer." It is a complete disease noun phrase in argument position, not an attributive noun. The surrounding risk-association frame ("associated with," "influence... risk") is semantically similar to the Modifier contexts ("ovarian cancer risk," "ovarian cancer population"). The model appears to have matched that epidemiological context and the repeated surface string instead of checking the syntactic role.
- **Hypothesis Check:** The single feature "prenominal attributive position vs. post-head/prepositional argument position" explains all cases. Example 1 is the reverse of the Modifier rule: it is a post-head PP complement, and the gold label is SpecificDisease. Its context does not change that, since the family-history and risk wording are not what determines the role.

**Step 2: Pattern Insight**

- **Pattern Name:** Disease Name as Prepositional Complement vs. Prenominal Attributive (Family-History Context Misfire)
- **Confusion Trigger:** A disease string inside a risk or family-history frame ("family history of ovarian cancer") is labelled Modifier because the model keys on the epidemiological context and the string's frequent prenominal use in the same document ("ovarian cancer cases/population/risk"), not on its syntactic role. "History of [disease]" looks like a qualifying descriptor, but the disease is the object of "of" and names the condition.
- **Contrastive Evidence:** The True Positive Modifiers occur before a head noun ("ovarian cancer population," "fragile X syndrome patients," "SLS genes"). The True Positive SpecificDiseases occur as subjects or after prepositions ("patients with SLS," "affected by Norrie disease," "Coats disease is characterized"). Example 1 matches the SpecificDisease pattern syntactically, which the model overlooked.
- **Linguistic Rule (Proposed):**
  1. Label a disease mention **Modifier** only when it is a prenominal attributive (noun-adjunct) that directly precedes and modifies a head noun, such as population, cases, study, patients, genes, protein, or risk, and is not itself governed by a preposition.
  2. Label a disease mention **SpecificDisease** when it is the head of an NP or the complement of a preposition or verb (e.g., "of X," "with X," "by X," or as a clause subject), even when the surrounding context is about family history, risk, or association.
  3. Apply the syntactic test first. Do not let the presence of risk or family-history vocabulary, or the same string appearing as a Modifier elsewhere in the document, override it.
moderation_principle:
### 1. Gold: SpecificDisease vs LLM: O (Missed) (8 cases)
- **Disease Named Without a Nosological Head:** IF a candidate span names a specific condition (through an eponym, proper name, or abbreviation) but its head noun is not a disease-class noun, and no nosological head or adjacent parenthetical expansion anchors it, THEN do not default to O. Label the full noun phrase, including any prepositional complement, as SpecificDisease when one of the following holds: (a) it is the complement of a causal or defining predicate that presents it as the identity of a condition named in the same sentence; (b) it is a sign or finding noun used as an alternate label for an eponymous condition already named in the document; or (c) it is a bare abbreviation whose expansion, stated elsewhere in the document, is a disease name.
  - **Negative constraint:** Do NOT apply when the phrase is a gene-level, enzyme-level, or laboratory observation that is not presented as defining a named disorder (for example, a mutation effect, a measured activity, or a cause of a different entity). Do NOT apply when the head is a broad category term, which remains DiseaseClass, or when the phrase contains only a Modifier (inheritance, severity, or age descriptor) without a disease name. Do NOT apply when the abbreviation's expansion refers to a gene, protein, assay, or drug rather than a disease.

### 2. Gold: DiseaseClass vs LLM: O (Missed) (2 cases)
- **Compositional Pathological-State Principle:**
  - **IF** a noun phrase combines a deviation-from-normal marker (an adjectival abnormality modifier, or a privative or deficiency prepositional phrase) with a generic biological substrate (a physiological process, anatomical structure, or molecular entity), **AND** the phrase denotes a pathological condition or state rather than normal variation or a laboratory measurement, **AND** the phrase is the argument of a disease-characterizing or causal predicate (for example, a "characterized by" or "results in" construction),
  - **THEN** tag the full span, including the deviation marker, as DiseaseClass. Do not tag the bare substrate (the process, structure, or molecule noun on its own).
  - **Negative Constraint:** Do NOT apply this rule when (a) the condition is a lexicalized, self-contained label with no qualifier-plus-substrate construction, which is tagged as a unit under the standard rule; (b) the substrate appears without a deviation marker and is described as normal physiology; (c) the deviation phrase describes an experimental manipulation, reagent state, or measurement without asserting a disease; or (d) the span is a coordinated multi-condition mention that belongs under CompositeMention.

### 3. Gold: DiseaseClass vs LLM: Modifier (Label Mismatch) (1 cases)
- **Principle: Disease mentions in prepositional complements are not Modifiers.**
  - **IF** a disease mention is the object of a prepositional complement (a noun phrase introduced by a preposition attached to a governing noun, such as a noun denoting history, risk, form, or the status of relatives or patients), **THEN** do not assign the Modifier label. Assign SpecificDisease if the mention names a particular disease entity, or DiseaseClass if it is a generic or unspecified category term with no named type.
  - **Modifier scope:** Reserve the Modifier label for a disease term that is an attributive premodifier immediately preceding a non-disease head noun, such as a noun denoting a population, study, risk, case, patient group, gene, or protein.
  - **Negative constraint:** This rule does **not** apply when the disease term is an attributive premodifier, because the Modifier label remains correct. It also does not apply when the prepositional phrase is internal to a single multi-token disease name, which takes its entity type as a unit, or when the disease mention is part of a coordinated structure governed by CompositeMention.
  - **Generalization:** The rule applies to any disease noun in the complement position of any preposition, regardless of the governing noun or the particular disease, as long as the disease noun is not serving as an attributive premodifier.

### 4. Gold: SpecificDisease vs LLM: Modifier (Label Mismatch) (1 cases)
- **Syntactic Role Overrides Surrounding Context for Disease Mentions**
  - **IF** a disease mention is the head of its own noun phrase, the complement of a preposition or verb, or a clausal subject (that is, it names the condition as an argument), **THEN** label it **SpecificDisease**, even when the sentence is framed around risk, association, family history, or epidemiology, and even when the identical string is labelled Modifier elsewhere in the document.
  - **IF** a disease mention is an unmarked prenominal noun-adjunct, not governed by a preposition, that directly precedes a head noun it characterizes (such as a population, case set, patient group, study, or gene), **THEN** label it **Modifier**.
  - **Decision order:** Apply the syntactic-role test first. Use lexical or topical cues only after the role is established.
  - **Negative constraint:** This rule does **not** apply when (a) the disease string is part of a larger span already governed by the DiseaseClass or CompositeMention definitions, since those definitions take precedence, or (b) the syntactic role is genuinely ambiguous, such as a noun-noun compound that could be either head or adjunct. In case (b), defer to the entity definitions rather than to how often the string is labelled Modifier in the document.

TEXT: Germline BRCA1 alterations in a population-based series of ovarian cancer cases.
The objective of this study was to provide more accurate frequency estimates of breast cancer susceptibility gene 1 ( BRCA1 ) germline alterations in the ovarian cancer population . To achieve this , we determined the prevalence of BRCA1 alterations in a population-based series of consecutive ovarian cancer cases . This is the first population-based ovarian cancer study reporting BRCA1 alterations derived from a comprehensive screen of the entire coding region . One hundred and seven ovarian cancer cases were analyzed for BRCA1 alterations using the RNase mismatch cleavage assay followed by direct sequencing . Two truncating mutations , 962del4 and 3600del11 , were identified . Both patients had a family history of breast or ovarian cancer . Several novel as well as previously reported uncharacterized variants were also identified , some of which were associated with a family history of cancer . The frequency distribution of common polymorphisms was determined in the 91 Caucasian cancer cases in this series and 24 sister controls using allele-specific amplification . The rare form of the Q356R polymorphism was significantly ( P = 0 . 03 ) associated with a family history of ovarian cancer , suggesting that this polymorphism may influence ovarian cancer risk . Coats disease is characterized by abnormal retinal vascular development ( so-called retinal telangiectasis ) which results in massive intraretinal and subretinal lipid accumulation ( exudative retinal detachment ) . The classical form of Coats disease is almost invariably isolated , unilateral and seen in males . A female with a unilateral variant of Coats disease gave birth to a son affected by Norrie disease . Subsequently analysis of the retinas of nine enucleated eyes from males with Coats disease demonstrated in one a somatic mutation in the NDP gene which was not present within non-retinal tissue . We suggest that Coats telangiectasis is secondary to somatic mutation in the NDP gene which results in a deficiency of norrin ( the protein product of the NDP gene ) within the developing retina . This supports recent observations that the protein is critical for normal retinal vasculogenesis .

Most fragile X syndrome patients have expansion of a ( CGG ) ( n ) sequence with > 200 repeats ( full mutation ) in the FMR1 gene responsible for this condition . Hypermethylation of the expanded repeat and of the FMR1 promoter is almost always present and apparently suppresses transcription , resulting in absence of the FMR1 protein . We recently showed that transcriptional reactivation of FMR1 full mutations can be achieved by inducing DNA demethylation with 5-azadeoxycytidine ( 5-azadC ) .
